title: Concretizing the Abstract Threat

part_a.trigger: The system presents security warnings or backup reminders in a generic, passive, and text-only manner (Visual Flaw) AND does so while the user is immersed in their ordinary workflow (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): A system message suggesting backup without showing the real impact of ransomware, leaving the risk as an abstract concept.
- Example 2 (Cloud Generalization): A corporate dashboard showing Security Status: 60% without explaining which specific files would be lost in the event of a breach.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This activates Cyber Risk Beliefs tied to unrealistic optimism (it will not happen to me). Without a tangible perception of severity, the user does not change their behavior.
part_a.error: The user physically clicks Dismiss or Remind me later to remove the interruption and return to their task.
part_a.mitigation: Nudge Bundle: Ingredient 1 (Response-Contingent Feedback - Revised) - The warning displays a blurred preview of the user personal files (e.g. photo folder or recent documents) to simulate the effect of ransomware. Important: to avoid alarm fatigue, activation must be restricted to cases where backup has been absent beyond critical thresholds (e.g. more than 7 days), and must always be paired with an immediately available action (Back up now). Ingredient 4 (Aversive Signals) - Use a high-contrast warning with loss-framing: Without a backup, you will permanently lose access to these 50 critical files.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify whether security notifications communicate the specific and tangible impact on the user data, or whether they remain in abstract technical terminology. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Enterprise: A message reading Backup not performed in 30 days appearing as a small grey icon in the system tray. Cloud: An Insecure DNS Configuration warning that does not explain the risk of personal email interception.
part_b.security_risk: The user perceives the risk as irrelevant to their personal situation. This leads to ignoring critical defenses in order to maintain operational speed.
part_b.remediation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle: use Dynamic Feedback (RCF) simulating data loss and Aversive Signals (loss-framing) to make the damage immediately understandable.
part_b.org_question: Does the organization provide post-attack psychological support to help employees manage stress and turn the incident into lasting awareness?

title: Legitimacy Validation through Visual Aesthetics

part_a.trigger: The system uses a semantically readable and clean URL (e.g. paypal.update-account.com) free of complex technical symbols (Visual Flaw) AND presents it while the user is focused on quickly completing a login or payment operation (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): The use of URLs such as www.paypal-hostding.com, perceived by users as clear and obvious compared to legitimate but long and complex URLs.
- Example 2 (Mobile Generalization - Revised): A system app requests the installation of a certificate named Android_Global_Trust_Fix.crt. The user trusts the familiar name without verifying its origin. The deception vector is twofold: beyond the name aesthetics, the implicit authority of the context also plays a role (the system itself is asking). The example should be understood as a variant of the base heuristic where visual trust is amplified by the perceived source. Methodological note: the error mechanism differs slightly from URL phishing as this is an active installation action, not a link click. Consider separating it into a distinct sub-example.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This triggers a distortion in Cyber Risk Beliefs. The user incorrectly believes that readability and visual order are indicators of security, while associating danger only with ugly or technical-looking interfaces.
part_a.error: The user physically clicks the action button (e.g. Login or Download) within the spoofed site instead of manually typing the official address or closing the page.
part_a.mitigation: Nudge Bundle: Ingredient 2 (Active Friction) - Insert a forced 3-second delay before allowing credential entry on infrequent external domains. Ingredient 3 (Social Cues) - Display a micro-message next to the action button: This domain has never been used by your colleagues. Verify the URL before proceeding.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify whether the system presents links or files with clean and familiar names that conceal technical discrepancies (e.g. double extensions or malicious third-level domains). (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Web: A portal displaying a link company-security.com pointing to an unverified external server. Mobile: A pop-up masking the real name of an installed package with the label Required Update.
part_b.security_risk: The interface leads the user to believe that readable equals safe. The user will click on dangerous links while ignoring technical warning signals.
part_b.remediation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle: add Active Friction (3-second delay) and Social Cues highlighting whether the domain is unknown to the organization.
part_b.org_question: Do internal policies explicitly distinguish between shortened links from approved tools (e.g. company-whitelisted shorteners) and unverified external links? Do employees know how to recognize this difference operationally?

title: Explicit Impact Mapping for Security Misconfigurations

part_a.trigger: The system allows the user to change a security-critical setting in an isolated text-field or toggle (Visual Flaw) AND it does not dynamically visualize the resulting change in the overall 'attack surface' or compliance status at the moment of the change (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): A Cloud dashboard where a user modifies a WAF rule. The system allows the change without alerting the user that this specific rule permits access to the Metadata Service.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A network admin tool where opening a port is treated as a simple 'on/off' switch without showing a map of which internal assets become visible to the public internet.
part_a.human_factor_exp: Users lack the 'Big Picture' of how a single technical change creates a 'Deadly Threat' as defined by Gupta et al.
part_a.error: The user will physically click 'Apply Changes' to fix a connectivity issue, unknowingly creating a massive security breach (e.g., making a private database public).
part_a.mitigation: Implement Effort Asymmetry (Friction) and Aversive Signals. For high-impact changes, the system must trigger a 'Consequence Modal' using high-contrast loss-framing (e.g., 'This change exposes 5 sensitive servers'). The user must wait for a 3-second countdown (Friction) before they can type 'I UNDERSTAND' to confirm the action.

part_b.audit_rule: Enforce Impact Awareness > Inspection Check: Verify if the interface dynamically shows the 'Security Impact' (e.g., exposed assets) during the configuration process or if it treats critical changes as simple, isolated toggles. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (Cloud): An S3 bucket settings page that allows 'Public Read Access' without displaying a high-contrast warning of exactly which files will be indexed by search engines.
- Domain B (IoT): A smart-device dashboard that allows disabling 'Secure Boot' with a single click, without explaining that this allows unsigned malicious firmware to run.
part_b.security_risk: Misconfiguration via Lack of Awareness. The user lacks the mental model to understand that a small UI change has a catastrophic security consequence.
part_b.remediation: Implement 'Impact-Friction'. When a high-risk toggle is flipped, present an Aversive Signal (red high-contrast warning) and require a 3-second 'cooling-off' period before the 'Apply' button becomes active.
part_b.org_question: Are administrators required to document the 'why' of a security change in a way that forces them to consider the risks?

title: Procedural Awareness Integration in Threat Validation

part_a.trigger: The system issues a high-level security warning (e.g., 'Suspicious Link Detected') providing only conceptual information about the risk (Visual Flaw) AND it fails to provide an immediate, 'in-place' mechanism for the user to perform a validation check before the final choice is made (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): An anti-phishing tool that marks an email as 'Suspicious' but does not offer a way to safely inspect the destination URL. The user is aware it might be phishing but lacks the procedure to verify it.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A mobile app requesting 'Accessibility Permissions' with a generic warning. The system provides no interactive guide or specific examples of what data the app will read, leaving the user with a 'conceptual' fear but no 'procedural' way to audit the app's intent.
part_a.human_factor_exp: According to Asanka & Love, conceptual knowledge alone does not increase self-efficacy; users need to know 'how' to perform the avoidance behavior.
part_a.error: The user will physically click 'Accept/Proceed anyway' within seconds because they lack the practical tools to validate the threat, leading to a 'forced' bypass of the security prompt.
part_a.mitigation: Implement Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF) and Social/Rule Cues. The interface must require the user to perform a 'Verification Ritual' (e.g., hover over a link for 2 seconds to reveal its true source). The 'Proceed' button remains locked until this RCF is triggered. Alongside, a Rule Cue should state: 'Company Policy 4.2 requires manual URL verification to prevent credential theft.'

part_b.audit_rule: Integrate Procedural Awareness > Inspection Check: Verify if the system, when flagging a threat, provides only a text warning or if it provides a functional 'check-step' (e.g., an inspection tool) that allows the user to verify the threat before deciding.
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (Email): A mail client warns 'External Sender' but provides no safe way to preview attachment metadata or link targets without opening them.
- Domain B (Mobile): An OS-level prompt asks for 'Full Disk Access' but does not show a 'View what this app will see' button, leaving the user procedurally blind.
part_b.security_risk: Lack of Procedural Awareness. The user knows there is a risk but doesn't know how to handle it, leading them to ignore the warning to finish their task.
part_b.remediation: Implement a 'Verification Bundle.' Use Active Friction (locking the 'Accept' button) until a Response-Contingent Feedback (e.g., a 2-second hover or a manual expansion of the URL) is completed. Pair this with a Rule Cue explaining the specific policy.
part_b.org_question: Does management penalize employees for the extra time spent using security verification tools?

title: Information-Siloed Security Reporting and Mitigation Failure

part_a.trigger: The system provides a flat, technical list of security vulnerabilities or error codes (Visual Flaw) AND it fails to provide immediate, contextualized actionable steps or copy-pasteable code snippets for remediation within the same report (Timing/Context Flaw)
part_a.examples:
- • Example 1 (Directly from Literature): A TLS scanner (like testssl.sh) that reports a server is "VULNERABLE" to CRIME or BREACH but does not explain that the fix involves disabling DEFLATE in specific Apache configuration files, forcing the admin to search external sources.
- • Example 2 (Generalization - Cloud/Enterprise): A Cloud Security dashboard flags a "Publicly Accessible Storage Bucket" but requires the administrator to navigate multiple sub-menus and external documentation to find the specific CLI command needed to restrict access.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers Cognitive Fatigue (Cognitive HF in MORPHEUS; a state of diminished mental capability resulting from prolonged engagement with demanding tasks). By forcing the professional to independently research, interpret technical jargon, and synthesize information from multiple external sources under time pressure, the Ul exhausts executive functions. This mental overload leads to a reliance on "System 1" automatic processing, resulting in concentration loss and suboptimal choices.
part_a.error: The user will physically leave a dangerous configuration active or apply a partial/incorrect patch (an omission or suboptimal choice) instead of implementing the full, correct security measure.
part_a.mitigation:
- • Ingredient 1: Rule Cues. The interface must provide "Actionable Mitigations": natural language explanations of the threat paired with ready-to-use code snippets and specific file path instructions directly next to the vulnerability.
- • Ingredient 2: Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF). The report should include a "Simulated Outcome" or preview button that allows the user to see the expected change in the security report (e.g., the "Vulnerable" status turning to "Safe") before they physically apply the configuration change.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if security vulnerability reports provide a flat list of technical defects without including immediate actionable mitigations, such as contextual explanations or ready-to-use code snippets. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (TLS Scanners): A report indicates a "CRIME" vulnerability but does not provide the specific Apache configuration lines required to disable TLS compression.
- Domain B (Cloud Admin): An enterprise dashboard flags a misconfigured firewall rule but requires the user to leave the interface to find the vendor-specific documentation for the fix.
part_b.security_risk: SECURITY RISK (Risk Profile): This interface induces Cognitive Fatigue. By forcing users to perform independent research and synthesize complex data from external sources, the Ul exhausts mental resources. Fatigued admins switch to "System 1" thinking and will leave configurations insecure or apply incorrect patches due to concentration loss and suboptimal decision-making.
part_b.remediation: 1_rule_cues : Embed natural language explanations and copy-pasteable code snippets directly within the vulnerability report. 2_rcf: Response-Contingent Feedback: Provide a "Dry-Run" preview that shows the user how the security status will change after the patch is applied.
part_b.org_question: ORGANIZATIONAL AUDIT QUESTION (Audit Context): "Does the company rely on employees' individual research to solve technical vulnerabilities, thereby ignoring the cognitive fatigue caused by information-gathering under pressure?"

title: Workload-Agnostic Security Design and Phishing Susceptibility

part_a.trigger: The system presents security warnings or administrative notifications using a static visual design AND it fails to adapt the delivery, timing, or prominence of these alerts based on the user's real-time workload intensity or documented peak operational windows
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Directly from Literature - Paper 1): Hospital staff receiving "announcements and other general notes" via email while simultaneously managing heavy patient loads or clinical emergencies. Because the system does not prioritize or delay these messages during peak times, overworked staff process them on "autopilot".
- Example 2 (Generalization): A corporate mobile app pushes a high-priority "Security Policy Update" alert using the same standard white pop-up used for benign social notifications while the user is in a high-stress environment (e.g., a busy commute), leading to a reflexive click just to clear the screen
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design actively induces Cognitive Fatigue (HF in the MORPHEUS model). This is a state of reduced mental capacity that occurs following prolonged engagement in cognitively demanding tasks. By remaining static and passive in the face of an overloaded user, the interface allows the brain to remain in an automatic and distorted "System 1" state, preventing the necessary transition to the deliberate and analytical thinking of "System 2."
part_a.error: The user will physically click on a malicious phishing link in less than 2 seconds (a reflexive action to "clear" the interface task) instead of performing a deliberate inspection of the sender's identity or the destination URL.
part_a.mitigation:
- • Ingredient 1: Effort Asymmetry (Active Friction). The system will implement a 3-second non-clickable delay on external links during peak workload hours to disrupt the automatic click loop
- • Ingredient 3 (Rule Cues): Display a clear behavioral prompt: "High Workload Detected: Avoid clicking links now. Use the 'Remind me in 1 hour' button to review this safely later."

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system presents security warnings or administrative notifications using a static visual design AND fails to adapt the delivery, timing, or prominence of these alerts based on the user's real-time workload intensity or documented peak operational windows. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations:
- - Domain A (Healthcare - Literature): Clinical staff receive a high volume of non-urgent administrative emails (e.g., general announcements) in the same format as critical alerts while simultaneously managing emergency patient intakes or heavy patient loads.
- Domain B (Corporate Mobile): A high-priority "Security Policy Update" alert is delivered via a standard white pop-up (identical to low-risk social notifications) while the user is in a high-stress environment, such as a busy commute.
part_b.security_risk: This design actively induces Cognitive Fatigue (Cognitive HF in the MORPHEUS model). Prolonged engagement in demanding tasks depletes mental resources, forcing the user into an automatic, distorted "System 1" state. As a result, the user will physically click on a malicious phishing link in less than 2 seconds, just to eliminate the distraction and return to their primary work.
part_b.remediation: 1. Active Friction Implement a 3-second non-clickable delay on external links during peak workload hours to disrupt the automatic click loop. 2. Rule Cues:  Display a dynamic prompt stating: "High Workload Detected: Avoid clicking links now. Use the 'Remind me in 1 hour' button to review this safely later.
part_b.org_question: 1. "Does the organization have a formal policy to limit 'extensive emailing' (e.g., non-urgent announcements) to reduce the daily cognitive load on staff?"

title: Disruption of Attentional Tunneling in Mobile Messaging

part_a.trigger: The system presents a notification or message containing a shortened or obscured URL, giving maximum visual emphasis to the 'Urgency' element (ex. 'Action required now!') (Visual Flaw) AND it does so without providing any native tool for safely previewing the link before physical interaction (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): An SMS from a delivery service (ex. USPS) reporting a 'held package' with a 'bit.ly link' or a misspelled URL (ex. post-it-delivery.com) that the user overlooks due to focus on the package issue.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A notification from a financial app stating 'Unauthorized access! Click here' where the mobile interface truncates the real address, preventing the user from seeing that the domain is not the official one.
part_a.human_factor_exp: The interface creates an 'attention tunnel' on the action (the click) rather than on reflection. Users with low attention spans or under superficial processing fail to analyze 'Message Attributes' (URL structure, sender) because technical details are hidden to maintain a cleaner UI.
part_a.error: The user will physically tap the link quickly within the first 2 seconds, instead of performing any safe inspection action (ex. long press to preview the full URL).
part_a.mitigation: Behavioral Bundle to force attention: 1. Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF): A pop-up highlighting the root domain in bold red requiring the user to enter the first three letters of the site to proceed. 2. Effort Asymmetry: Disabling direct clicks from unknown senders, forcing a 2-second long-press to activate the link.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify whether the system presents links or CTAs using shortened, obscured, or truncated URLs, visually prioritizing urgency without providing a built-in inspection or mandatory link preview before opening.
part_b.violations: Domain A: Delivery notification containing 'bit.ly/3xYz' without destination domain info. Domain B: Push notification displaying only 'Tap to secure your account', completely hiding the target web address.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces a decline in Cognitive Reflexivity focused on Attention. The user's focus is directed exclusively to emotional content (urgency), leading to impulsive tapping that bypasses security knowledge.
part_b.remediation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle: 1. Effort Asymmetry (require long press to activate link). 2. Response-Contingent Feedback (clear preview of the root domain in contrasting color with explicit confirmation required).
part_b.org_question: Does the organization conduct phishing tests that vary based on message complexity (ex. shortened vs. long URLs) to identify susceptibility to attentional tunneling under pressure?

title: Disruption of Deceptive Fluency in Identity Verification

part_a.trigger: The system presents a high-risk request for action (e.g. a link) by perfectly mimicking the style and sender of trusted communications (Visual Flaw) AND it does so without interrupting the user's natural reading flow (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): An SMS appearing in a previously legitimate conversation (with the same sender ID) that says 'Your account has been blocked, click here to unblock,' prompting the user to click on a link that redirects to a clone website.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A messaging app (such as Telegram) that allows external bots to send fake 'System Notifications' messages with the text structure, profile picture, and description consistent with the app's standard notifications.
part_a.human_factor_exp: The design exploits the lack of analytical reflection (low TRDM), and the user processes information heuristically (automatically and quickly) rather than systematically, skipping situation evaluation and analysis of alternatives.
part_a.error: The user physically clicks on the malicious link instead of ignoring the message and opening the banking app to check the account status or other reported communications.
part_a.mitigation: Implementation of an 'Active Friction' Behavioral Bundle: 1. Effort Asymmetry (e.g., a full-screen overlay with a slider to proceed) to interrupt the natural flow. 2. Social/Rule Cues (e.g., a message stating 'Security policy requires manual review for unidentified external links').

part_b.audit_rule: Verify whether the system presents links or requests for critical action within messages that mimic the visual and textual identity of trusted communications without inserting physical interruptions or 'disfluency' cues.
part_b.violations: Domain A: SMS in official banking queue requesting data update via link without OS/app reporting external nature. Domain B: Admin panel with 'Password Expiration' button identical to routine notifications.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces low Cognitive Reflexivity. The user processes the threat through rapid/heuristic thinking (System 1) leading to an impulsive action that bypasses consideration of consequences.
part_b.remediation: Implement an 'Active Friction' Behavioral Bundle: 1. Introduce effort asymmetry (e.g., confirmation slider or 3-second timer). 2. Display a dynamic rule cue to force a shift to analytical thinking.
part_b.org_question: Does the company monitor whether phishing test error rates are tied to specific employee cognitive profiles (ex. impulsiveness) and adjust technical controls accordingly?

title: Prevention of Automation Bias in Complex Transactions

part_a.trigger: The interface presents a cryptographic authorization request or a transaction omitting to translate the technical data into readable language (Visual Flaw), and does so during a process driven by speculation, hype, or strict time limits (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): A poorly designed and complex interface for trading NFTs that requires the user to sign a smart contract without clearly explaining which assets they are granting access to, causing fatal operational errors.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Mobile Banking): A traditional banking app that shows the terms of an international wire transfer in a dense tabular format of routing and SWIFT codes, pushing the user to blindly click the large green "Confirm" button without reading.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This triggers an Automation/Default Bias. Due to the "blockchain trust paradox" (trust is built into the technology but is not clearly experienced by the user), the user gives up in the face of complexity and blindly trusts the interface, assuming the default action is safe.
part_a.error: The user will physically approve the malicious transaction or click "Sign" in the wallet without verifying the granted permissions.
part_a.mitigation: Use Response-Contingent Feedback and Active Friction. The system must translate the technical complexity into an immediate visual summary of the consequences (e.g., "You are about to transfer ownership of X"). If the transaction deviates from the user's habitual patterns, the interface must hide the default "Confirm" button and require the user to type the exact amount or a keyword before unlocking it.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the interface presents an authorization request (e.g., system permissions or cryptographic transactions) omitting to translate complex technical data into a readable language (Visual Flaw), and if it does so during a process driven by strict time limits, speculation, or goal-oriented workflows (Timing/Context Flaw). (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A (Web3/NFT): A poorly designed interface for trading NFTs that requires the user to sign a smart contract without clearly explaining in natural language which assets they are granting access to, causing operational errors. | Domain B (Mobile Banking/Fintech): A banking app that shows the terms of an international wire transfer in a dense tabular format of incomprehensible SWIFT codes, presenting a huge green "Confirm" button that pushes the user to blindly click to overcome the obstacle.
part_b.security_risk: This interface triggers the Automation Bias (or Default Bias). Due to cognitive overload and the incomprehensibility of the technical data, the user gives up and blindly trusts the system. The user will physically approve the transaction or click on "Sign/Allow" without verifying the permissions, mistakenly assuming that the default highlighted action is safe.
part_b.remediation: Use a "Behavioral Bundle" with Response-Contingent Feedback and Active Friction. The system must translate the complexity into an immediate visual summary (e.g., icons showing what goes in and out of the wallet). If the transaction is anomalous or high-risk, the interface must remove the default "Confirm" button and require an intentional physical action from the user, such as typing the exact amount or the word "APPROVE" to unlock the operation.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Is the design/development team evaluated based on metrics that favor a "frictionless" user experience to increase operation completion volumes, sacrificing the clarity of security information?

title: Prevention of Truth Bias in Familiar Interfaces

part_a.trigger: The system presents a link or a social engineering message using the exact same visual format (layout, font, colors) as legitimate messages from trusted contacts (Visual Flaw), and does so in a context of fast scrolling or habitual use of the social network (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): A fake message from a friend on a social network that exploits the familiarity of the environment to make the user click on a malicious link, completely bypassing critical attention.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Enterprise): An enterprise messaging app like Teams that shows a malicious link sent by a compromised or external account with the same reassuring visual preview as verified internal links.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers Truth Bias and heuristic processing. Believing in the honesty of others is a default automatic cognitive state that simplifies social interactions, leading the user to mistake threats for truth within a familiar environment.
part_a.error: The user will physically click on the link or automatically share the post without adequate cognitive processing.
part_a.mitigation: Implement a 'Behavioral Bundle' using Effort Asymmetry and Social/Rule Cues. When the user clicks on an unverified external link, the system must block the immediate redirection, inserting friction (e.g., a mandatory 3-second timer) and showing a microcopy that breaks the visual homogeneity indicating a clear rule (e.g., 'You are leaving the trusted network, verify the URL').

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system presents an external link or a potential social engineering message using the exact same visual format (layout, font, colors) as legitimate messages from trusted contacts (Visual Flaw), and if it does so in a context of fast scrolling or habitual platform use where analytical attention is low (Timing/Context Flaw). (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A (Social Media): A fake message from a friend on a social network that exploits the familiarity of the environment to make the user click on a malicious link, completely bypassing critical attention. | Domain B (Enterprise): An enterprise messaging app (e.g., Slack or Teams) that shows a malicious link sent by a compromised account with the same reassuring standard visual preview used for safe links sent by colleagues.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces Truth Bias and heuristic processing of information. The user relies on the familiar environment and the 'truth-default' (automatically believing that the message is legitimate). Consequently, the user will physically click on the link or automatically share the post in less than a second, without performing a critical analysis of the source.
part_b.remediation: Implement a 'Behavioral Bundle'. When a user clicks on an unverified external link in a familiar environment, the system must block the immediate redirection (Effort Asymmetry/Friction via a mandatory 3-second timer) and show a microcopy that breaks visual homogeneity indicating a clear rule (Social/Rule Cue: 'You are leaving the trusted network, verify the URL before proceeding').
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization evaluate or reward employees for response speed and 'real-time' communication, effectively reducing the time available to them for the systematic analysis of messages?

title: Informed password selection and friction

part_a.trigger: The system provides only static password requirements without explaining why a password is weak or providing actionable guidance based on the user's input (Visual Flaw) AND it fails to provide meaningful feedback during password creation that helps the user understand how to improve their password (Timing/Context Flaw)
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): Corporate portals suggest general rules like using at least 8 characters or a number. These systems fail to provide specific heuristics during the selection, leading to passwords that are still very weak even if they satisfy portal requests.
- Example 2 (Generalization-Mobile): Applications, despite showing a metric for password strength, still allows users to select weak passwords.
part_a.human_factor_exp: Generic recommendations about password strength reinforce the Lack of Knowledge human factor by creating an illusion of competence. Users believe that satisfying basic requirements (e.g., symbols, length) is sufficient, without understanding underlying risks such as predictability or reuse.
part_a.error: The user will keep selecting weak passwords or the same password for different accounts, ignoring the risk.
part_a.mitigation: Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF). The system provides interactive messages based on the user input to guide him in building a password that is actually strong. Effort Asymmetry (Friction). If a user tries to proceed with a weak password, a pop-up appears, forcing a choice: the user can either go back to strengthen the password or explicitly accept the risk after reading about potential consequences, such as identity theft or financial fraud.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system relies only on static password requirements (e.g., length, symbols) without explaining why a password is weak. Furthermore, verify if the system does not provide contextual and actionable feedback during password creation to help the user improve their password. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A: A registration form accepts passwords as strong ones based only on length and symbols, without warning about common patterns. Domain B: The app shows a color-based strength meter (red/green) without explaining why the password is weak or how to improve it. Domain C (Enterprise): A corporate system enforces complex rules but provides no feedback beyond 'Password does not meet requirements', forcing users to guess what to change.
part_b.security_risk: Users are likely to believe their passwords are secure when they actually follow predictable patterns. Without specific guidance, users prioritize speed over security, leading to poor password hygiene and increased vulnerability to credential-stuffing attacks.
part_b.remediation: Implement an interactive meter that updates in real-time, including a "time-to-crack" estimate or a warning if the password contains common patterns. Replace long, static lists of requirements with adaptive hints that appear only when a specific rule is violated. When a weak password is detected, present a choice that highlights the loss. For example: "Do you want to go back and strengthen your password, or do you want to accept the risk of identity theft and financial fraud?"
part_b.org_question: "Does the organization provide a modern strength metric that explains why a password is weak, and do the employees understand and trust adopted security tools?”

title: Security Education through embedded dynamical visual cues and concrete directly applicable suggestions

part_a.trigger: The system shows informative security banners or modal with general recommendations against phishing emails [Visual Flaw] AND it presents them during low-stakes moments, rather than at the specific point of interaction with a potential threat [Timing/Context Flaw].
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): Despite the presence of cues such as the discrepancy between the display name and the actual address, syntax irregularities, and malformed URLs, users with low technical knowledge fail to engage correctly in email elaboration and general warnings are not enough to protect the user.
- Example 2 (Generalization-Mail app): Mail app shows persistent banner 'Be careful with external links'.
- Example 3 (Generalization-Bank apps): Banking applications often deploy generic anti-fraud modal pop-ups immediately upon app launching. This is an anti-pattern because it provides security information in a low-stakes context and since the user is not currently performing a sensitive operation, they lack the immediate motivation to process the information and acquire the needed knowledge which facilitate email elaboration.
part_a.human_factor_exp: Generic and out-of-context warnings fail to trigger the user's functional knowledge. This leads to a Lack of Knowledge outcome because the user might have shallow awareness that frauds exist, but the UI fails to explicitly provide the specific cues to look for during an actual threat. Consequently, the user does not learn how to distinguish signal from noise and will more likely fail to engage in email elaboration, since they have no useful information about what to look for.
part_a.error: The user will dismiss the pop-up/warning in less than 1 second without having the necessary information to process the email content and will subsequently engage in reading the email without verifying the sender's domain or inspecting the link structure.
part_a.mitigation: Studies indicate that general warnings or even training are insufficient. The waning effect probably occurs because traditional education is typically detached from the specific moment a user must make a critical decision. Nudges consisting of short and directly applicable information provided at the right time demonstrate higher efficacy. Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF). Security tools provide dynamic feedback during email interaction by integrating features like a suspicion score, which visually updates or changes color based on the specific content of the email to reflect real-time risk levels. Effort Asymmetry (Friction). The system displays the history of previous interactions with a sender, including date, time and subject line, or, if no history exists, prompts the user to verify if the communication was expected while providing a direct link for external verification on Google. Furthermore, classifying emails by their underlying intent before they are opened is useful since the user tends to focus on the content. Social/Rule Cues. The system displays alerts such as “Five colleagues have reported this email as suspicious” or by providing "check" buttons that allow users to review IT security heuristics and view a technical dissection of URLs in the emails.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system presents generic, non-specific security warnings (e.g., 'Be careful with external links') without indicating concrete cues to inspect. Furthermore, verify if these warnings are shown outside the critical decision-making moment rather than being embedded directly within the user's interaction with a potentially malicious email. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A: Email app shows a permanent banner "Be careful with external links". Domain B: The system asks a user to "Check existing emails from this sender" but doesn't show directly the list of previous interactions and the user must leave the email and manually search the history
part_b.security_risk: This interface assumes prior user expertise and fails to provide actionable knowledge at the moment of need. Users remain unable to identify concrete phishing cues and will process emails superficially, leading to uninformed and potentially dangerous decisions.
part_b.remediation: Implement Just-in-Time Security Nudges. Provide embedded, contextual cues directly within the email interface (e.g., highlight sender domain mismatches, suspicious links, or lack of prior interaction). Pair these cues with actionable shortcuts (e.g., one-click access to interaction history). Introduce lightweight friction only during high-risk actions and include short, directly applicable heuristics (e.g., 'Does the domain match the official source?'). Avoid generic and out-of-context warnings.
part_b.org_question: "Does the organization provide 'Just-in-Time' tools to help employees dissect threats, or does it rely solely on annual training that is disconnected from the actual workflow?"

title: Prevention of Password Transformation Complacency

part_a.trigger: The system uses static dialing rules or a password strength indicator that visually validates security (e.g. green tick) as soon as the required special character is entered (Visual/Interaction Flaw), and does so without performing any dynamic checks to verify whether the password is a simple and predictable structural transformation (e.g. adding a number at the end) compared to common patterns (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (From Literature): A web service prompts you to add a number, and the user changes his standard password from "password" to "password1", a transformation that cross-site guessing algorithms guess almost immediately.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Enterprise): A company dashboard forces employees to change their password every 90 days; the system accepts the new password because the user simply incremented the last number (e.g. from "Company2023" to "Company2024").
- Example 3 (Generalization - Mobile): A financial app requires the creation of a 6-digit PIN, and the system accepts without warning the insertion of trivial sequential patterns on physical keyboards (e.g., "123456" or "qwerasdf" converted to numbers) that simulate complexity.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers Complacency. The user expresses unfounded confidence in the sufficiency of his or her minimum effort. By satisfying the rule imposed by the interface (e.g., adding a symbol), he feels a sense of complacency that nullifies the real awareness of the risk of attacks based on dictionaries and transformation rules.
part_a.error: The user will physically type in a password that is a trivial structural variation of a password already in use (e.g. adding a number at the end) instead of generating or typing a cryptographically unique and secure string.
part_a.mitigation: **Description**: Implement a "Behavioral Bundle" based on dynamic controls. The system must cross-reference the input with known transformation models or dictionaries (Response-Contingent Feedback) in real time. If it detects a lazy variation, the system will not only reject the password, but will introduce Active Friction by blocking the form for 3 seconds, accompanied by a contextual Rule Cue : "This password follows an overly predictable pattern (e.g. number at the end). For security policies, passwords must be unique and free of common patterns."

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system relies on static composition rules or meters that visually validate the password as soon as a required character is typed (Visual/Interaction Flaw), AND it does so without dynamically checking if the password is a simple, predictable transformation (e.g., adding a number at the end) of common patterns (Timing/Context Flaw). (Pass/Fail)
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (Web): A registration form highlights the password strength as "Strong" simply because the user capitalized the first letter and added a "1" at the end of a dictionary word.
- Domain B (Enterprise): An Active Directory password reset prompt allows the user to satisfy the 90-day rotation policy by simply changing "Admin2023!" to "Admin2024!".
- Domain C (Mobile): A mobile app accepts a 6-digit PIN that is a direct, simple transformation of sequential keyboard strokes without triggering a warning.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces Complacency. Users will develop an unfounded belief that their minimal effort is sufficient and will physically type a predictably transformed password (e.g., appending a digit) instead of creating a truly unique credential, leaving the account highly vulnerable to cross-site guessing algorithms.
part_b.remediation: Implement Dynamic Transformation Checks. Introduce a Behavioral Bundle combining Response-Contingent Feedback (real-time checking against known transformation patterns) with Active Friction (e.g., a 3-second delay on rejection) and a Rule Cue stating explicitly: "This password follows a highly predictable pattern used by attackers. You must create a unique phrase."
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the company rely on outdated static password composition rules that encourage lazy user transformations, rather than verifying passwords against compromised lists and known hacking patterns?

title: Prevention of Complacency in Link Inspection

part_a.trigger: The system displays a superficial and easily falsifiable trust indicator (such as the sender's display name or HTTPS padlock icon) by hiding the real address or destination URL behind a generic text link (Visual Flaw), and it does so in a context where the user is handling a large volume of emails or routine messages (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (From Literature): A corporate email client only shows the name "IT Helpdesk" to make the interface cleaner, omitting to show that the real email is a typosquatting domain (e.g. support@microsoft-update.com instead of microsoft.com). The experienced user clicks feeling confident in the display name.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Mobile): Due to limited space, a mail app on smartphones completely hides the URL on hover (hover not possible), forcing the user to rely solely on the link text ("Click here to track the package").
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers Complacency. The user, especially if they are familiar with the technology, overestimates their ability to recognize threats or assumes that they are not a target. This unfounded sense of security blocks critical analysis (System 2) and leads the user to trust the most obvious and deceptive visual elements, ignoring hidden discrepancies.
part_a.error: The user will physically and impulsively click on the malicious link in less than 2 seconds, instead of performing the safe action of inspecting the real URL (e.g. doing a "hovering" action with the mouse or expanding the sender's details).
part_a.mitigation: **Description**: Implement a "Behavioral Bundle" on emails coming from the outside. The system will use a Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF): when you hover over the link, an interactive high-contrast tooltip will visually break down the URL highlighting the real domain. If the domain is unknown, Active Friction will be added: by clicking on the link, the system will block the page from loading for 3 seconds showing a Rule Cue : "This link takes you out of the company network. Please verify the domain highlighted in red before proceeding."

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system displays superficial trust indicators (like a sender's display name or generic hyperlink text) while hiding the actual source email address or destination URL by default (Visual Flaw), AND it does so in a context where the user processes a high volume of routine messages (Timing/Context Flaw). (Pass/Fail)
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (Desktop Email): An email client renders the sender's name as "HR Department" in large, bold font, but completely hides the actual sending email address inside a collapsed "Details" dropdown menu.
- Domain B (Mobile UI): A messaging app on a smartphone displays a hyperlink simply as "Login here" and provides no mechanism (like long-press preview) to inspect the true URL before the physical tap occurs.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces Complacency, particularly among users who consider themselves tech-savvy. Overestimating their own security posture, users will bypass analytical thinking and physically click the malicious link in less than two seconds instead of verifying the hidden true destination.
part_b.remediation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle. Combine Response-Contingent Feedback (a high-contrast tooltip that visually breaks down and highlights the true domain when hovering over a link) with Active Friction (a 3-second delay popup for external links) and a Rule Cue stating: "External Domain Warning: You are leaving the corporate network. Verify the domain."
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization's communication foster complacency by making employees believe that the automated firewall/antispam catches 100% of threats, thus discouraging them from manually inspecting links?

title: Prevention of Experts' Overconfidence via Temporal Friction

part_a.trigger: The system utilizes a static toggle switch, basic checkbox, or open-ended dropdown to allow privileged users to temporarily disable a critical security control or grant a global exception (Visual Flaw) AND it does so without enforcing a mandatory system-automated expiration parameter or displaying a disruptive, persistent indicator while the risky state is active (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (From Literature - Endpoint Security): As documented by Rahman et al. (2024, p. 69, Table 8), an antivirus/endpoint system allows an administrator to click a 'Disable Protection' toggle to run a blocked legitimate script (Exception Handling). The system relies entirely on the admin to manually return and flip the toggle back on later.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Cloud Infrastructure): A cloud firewall console allows a network engineer to add a temporary 'Allow All (0.0.0.0/0)' rule to troubleshoot an SSH connection, using the exact same standard UI row as permanent rules, with no auto-expiry constraint.
- Example 3 (Generalization - Identity & Access): An internal dashboard allows an admin to manually elevate a user's privileges to 'Admin' for a quick ad-hoc fix, utilizing a basic dropdown menu that lacks the automated expiration features of true Just-In-Time (JIT) access systems.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers a specific subset of Overconfidence in expert users known as the Prospective Memory Illusion. High technical expertise generates an inflated, uncalibrated self-assurance in the user's own cognitive capacity (i.e., the overconfident belief that 'I am a professional doing a 5-minute task; I won't forget to turn the firewall back on'). Because they systematically overestimate their ability to remember future intentions, they treat system-enforced safety protocols as unnecessary bureaucratic hurdles and bypass them, relying instead on their flawed, overconfident memory.
part_a.error: Driven by an overestimation of their own prospective memory, the user will physically click the 'Disable/Bypass' toggle for a temporary task, subsequently abandon the session when the task is complete, and fail to physically return to the menu to re-enable the control leaving the system permanently exposed.
part_a.mitigation: Implement a Cognitive Wedge Bundle that completely eliminates the system's reliance on the expert's overconfident memory. Ingredient 1: Effort Asymmetry (Time-Bound Friction). Remove the static 'on/off' toggle for security exceptions. To disable a control, the system must force the user to physically input a specific duration for the bypass (e.g., typing '30m' or selecting from a mandatory time-bound dropdown). The system must automatically revert to the secure state when the timer expires. Ingredient 2: Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF). While the exception is active, the interface must display a persistent, high-contrast countdown timer (e.g., 'Warning: Firewall Exception Active - Auto-reverting in 14:59'). Crucially, to counter the 'Fatigue' and desensitization documented by Rahman et al. (Table 5, p. 68), this banner must visually disrupt the normal workflow (e.g., pinned to the top of the viewport, physically pushing functional content down) rather than sitting passively in a notification bell.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system utilizes a static toggle switch, checkbox, or open-ended dropdown to allow privileged users to temporarily disable a critical security control or create an exception (Visual Flaw) AND it does so without enforcing a mandatory system-automated expiration parameter or displaying a disruptive, persistent indicator while the risky state is active (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_b.violations: Domain A (Enterprise/Endpoint): An administrative console allows IT staff to pause the antivirus or execution restrictions on a machine by right-clicking and selecting 'Suspend Protection,' relying purely on the admin's memory to turn it back on. Domain B (Cloud/Network): A cloud security group interface allows engineers to insert a temporary 'Allow All' inbound rule to troubleshoot connectivity without requiring an expiration timer, causing the rule to become a permanent vulnerability. Domain C (Identity Management): A system allows admins to manually elevate a standard user to a high-privilege role for a specific task using a basic dropdown, with no automated system to downgrade the user afterward (failing to implement true JIT access constraints).
part_b.security_risk: This interface feeds Expert Overconfidence. Highly skilled users systematically overestimate their prospective memory (the ability to remember future actions). By relying on human memory rather than system constraints, the interface allows the user to physically disable protection for a 'quick task.' Driven by overconfidence, the user will inevitably fail to re-enable it once distracted, leaving the infrastructure permanently exposed to cyberattacks.
part_b.remediation: Implement a Temporal Friction Bundle. Replace binary 'On/Off' toggles for security bypasses with Time-Bound Friction: force the admin to explicitly set a time limit (e.g., 15 minutes) before the bypass is granted, after which the system automatically reverts to the secure state. To combat user 'Fatigue' (Rahman et al., 2024), combine this with Response-Contingent Feedback by displaying a highly disruptive, persistent countdown banner globally across the UI while the exception is active.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization prioritize rapid ticket resolution metrics (like MTTR) for IT staff in a way that creates time pressure? Time pressure reliably amplifies overconfidence, incentivizing staff to take shortcuts and rely on their flawed memory to 'clean up exceptions later' when modifying firewall rules, disabling endpoint protection, or assigning manual privileges.

title: Prevention of Selective-Processing Overconfidence via Sequential Task Coupling

part_a.trigger: The system scatters multiple independent technical security indicators (e.g., origin address, digital signature status, embedded link URLs) across disparate, peripheral zones of the interface (Visual Flaw) AND it presents the primary action button concurrently, allowing immediate execution without guiding the user's attention sequentially to all relevant indicators (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature - Email/Phishing): An email client shows the sender's familiar name at the top left, but the actual hyperlink destination is only visible in a tiny status bar at the bottom left when hovering, splitting attention across the screen (Wang et al., 2016).
- Example 2 (Generalization - Mobile/Banking): A mobile banking app highlights the payee's name in massive bold text at the center, but places the modified destination IBAN number in small, light-grey font at the bottom of a scrollable view.
- Example 3 (Generalization - Enterprise/DevOps): A deployment dashboard displays a large green 'Build Ready' banner prominently, while the critical warning regarding an unsigned dependency is buried in an unexpanded side-panel tab.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers Overconfidence by exploiting Variability in Attention Allocation. As proven by Wang et al. (2016, pp. 766, 772; Hypothesis 2), scattered cues lead users to engage in 'selective processing,' where they lock onto confirming evidence (familiar names) and neglect disconfirming evidence in peripheral zones.
part_a.error: The user will physically click the 'Execute,' 'Transfer,' or 'Allow' button in less than a second after scanning only a single confirming visual cue, instead of physically moving their eyes to verify all scattered security indicators.
part_a.mitigation: Implement a Sequential Task Coupling Bundle: 1. Effort Asymmetry (Active Friction): Disable the primary action button by default. 2. Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF): Require the user to physically interact with/checkbox each indicator sequentially; a visual progress meter fills until the action button unlocks. 3. Rule Cues: Place microcopy stating: 'Security Policy: All indicators must be individually verified.'

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if multiple independent technical security indicators are scattered across peripheral zones (Visual Flaw) AND if the action button is active before the user is guided to each indicator (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_b.violations: Browser warning titles placed top-center with certificate details in collapsed bottom-left tabs; financial apps placing 'Approve' buttons immediately below the amount while hiding destination details off-screen.
part_b.security_risk: This induces Overconfidence through Selective Processing. Users will selectively process only the most salient, confirming cues and click 'Approve' with high confidence while ignoring buried disconfirming evidence.
part_b.remediation: Implement a Sequential Task Coupling Bundle. Lock the 'Approve' button (Active Friction) and introduce a step-by-step workflow (RCF) that requires the user to interact with each indicator (origin, signature, destination) before the final action is unlocked.
part_b.org_question: Does the organization's training program rely on simplified scenarios that artificially highlight malicious cues, failing to prepare users for complex attention-allocation tasks?

title: Aligning user perception with service criticality

part_a.trigger: The system uses identical login interfaces both for routine and sensitive services [Visual Flaw] AND the transition between low-risk and high-risk services occurs without any contextual cue signalling the change in the risk level [Context Flaw].
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): An expert of the FAA (Federal Aviation Administration) has the access to the system that controls the radars and all the administrative routine tasks (access to the turns of the next weeks, punch its badge, require some days off, …); since the system presents the same authentication interface for all services, he may misinterpret the level of risk associated with the radar control service, perceiving it as comparable to routine administrative tasks.
- Example 2 (Generalization): The system used by the doctors of an hospital provides several services: it allows to consult the plan of the surgical interventions they will carry out in the following days, the canteen menu, as well as the medical records of each single patient, with all data about his health status; a doctor, since these services are accessed with the same log-in interface, may interpret the access to the patient data as a routine operation, wrongly perceiving the level of risk associated with this operation.
part_a.human_factor_exp: The Morpheus human factor triggered in this context is the misperception; since the authentication procedure is the same for high-risk services and routine operations, the user may incorrectly interpret the importance of the accessed service and he may underestimate the consequences of a credential violation and perceive the security policies as unnecessary.
part_a.error: The user will use the same simple password for routine and sensitive services [Action] instead of creating and maintaining stronger credentials for critical tasks [Safe action].
part_a.mitigation: If the authentication interface for all the low-risk services can be left unchanged, some modifications must be applied to the login page of the critical services. First of all, to introduce an active friction, the system must require the user to authenticate himself in the service by using a 2FA method, so that he is actively involved into the authentication process and forced to interpret it as a non-routine service. (Friction) The system should introduce a banner to indicate that the user is logging into a service that requires a safety-critical session and a bar will show the level of risk of the service to which the user is logging in, compared to all the others provided by the system. (Response-Contingent Feedback).

part_b.audit_rule: Prevent risk misevaluation (misperception) > Inspection check: verify if the system uses the same login interface for both low-risk and sensitive services. Furthermore, check if the system provides contextual indicators of the risk level for each one of the services supplied.
part_b.violations: Domain A (Aviation): a system used for monitoring radars and execute all employee’s routine tasks has the same authentication interface for all its services, and this let the users perceive the critical services like routine tasks and reduce their attention in using secure credentials. Domain B (Hospital): an hospital digital system uses the same login interface both for routine operations (for example showing the daily canteen menu, consulting the scheduled surgical interventions of the next weeks, …) and to access to the sensitive patient medical records; since the two interfaces are not distinguishable, doctors may distort the perception of real risks of attacks on the services, violating the hospital’s policies on passwords.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces misperception because when the authentication interface is identical for routine and sensitive services, users may misperceive the real security risks for these services and this may lead them to violate secure policies defined by the company; as a result, users may use the same password for more services with different levels of risk.
part_b.remediation: It should be introduced into the authentication page for accessing safety-critical systems a 2FA mechanism, so that the effort required to access sensitive services will be greater than the routine ones; the interface should also display a banner to inform the users that they are logging into a service that requires a safety-critical session and a visual indicator that highlight the criticality of the accessed service compared to the others provided by the system.
part_b.org_question: during the management interview, ask: Does the organization require employees to access both routine and sensitive services under time pressure, potentially encouraging them to treat the authentication procedures as a routine? Does the organization have some training programs for users who still have not understood the rigid privacy policies introduced in the company or also to introduce them secure credential managers?

title: The extension masking in trusted communication channels

part_a.trigger: The system doesn’t show the type of the file in the file name, representing file type only through icons [Visual Flaw] AND it does so when users download or open attachments of messages coming from the company’s mail domain [Context Flaw].
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): An operating system (such as Windows) that, by default, deactivates the visualization of file extensions and users can only rely on icons to detect the type of file; but the file icon can be manipulated to not really reflect the type of the file.
- Example 2 (Generalization): Considering a cloud system in which a group of users share a folder, when a user upload a new file into the folder, a notification is sent to all the users that have the desktop client of the cloud service installed on their computers; the notification just present the name of the file (without its real extension), and the icon of the software that (should) be used to open it.
part_a.human_factor_exp: The Morpheus human factor triggered in this context is the misperception, because the icon associated with the file may let the user interpret the malicious file as a harmless document, given that the system doesn’t show him the extension of the attachment in its name.
part_a.error: The user will open the preview of the file or download it and open it offline just relying on the graphical icon shown [Action] instead of inspecting the details of the attachment received in the message to verify if the extension of the file really matches the icon [Safe Action].
part_a.mitigation: Implement “Active warnings”: a thick and colored border will circle the icon associated with a file so that, when an attachment has a potentially dangerous extension, it will be colored of orange/red, according to the damages that a file with this extension may cause. (Aversive Signals combined with Response-Contingent Feedback). In order to avoid clicks on dangerous attachments, when a file with a potentially dangerous extension is opened or downloaded by the user, a pop-up will explain the potential danger that a file of this kind may carry out and it will be required to the user to click on the button Confirm in the case in which he wants to continue opening or downloading the file, on Cancel otherwise. (Effort Asymmetry)

part_b.audit_rule: The extension masking (Misperception) > Inspection Check: verify if the system hides the real extension of files or it represents the type of the files just using graphic icons; furthermore, verify if this lack of transparency happens during the downloading or the opening of the attachments of email messages coming from an email address of the company’s domain.
part_b.violations: Domain A (Web/Email): a mailing client that, for the messages coming from addresses of the company’s domain, shows the preview of the files or allows their download without visualizing the real extensions of the attachments; Domain B (Operating Systems): an operating system (like Windows) that, by default, deactivates the visualization of file extensions, so that the users can only rely on graphic icons, which can easily be manipulated; Domain C (Cloud): a cloud collaboration platform that sends the notifications related to new or modified items of a shared folder just showing the name of the file (without the real extension) and the icon of the software with which it should be opened.
part_b.security_risk: The interface induces misperception, because users may interpret malicious files as a harmless document due to the graphic icon that indicates the software with which it should be opened, but the icon has been manipulated by attackers; as a consequence, the user will open or download the attachment, by omitting the inspection of the file details.
part_b.remediation: Implement active warnings that will circle the icon that indicates the software with which an attachment with suspicious extension will be opened. It will also be introduced an active friction that forces the user to press a confirmation button to open one of the suspicious attachments of a message, in order to break the automatic process in the user’s mind; the pop-up with the button must also contain an explanation of the most dangerous risks a file with this extension can generate.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization have a discipline program for all employees who take time to review the details of each document received and verify the sender's credibility and, consequently, are slower to complete their tasks? Does it exist a training plan to help users learning to manage the active frictions imposed by the system to avoid opening files with potentially dangerous extensions? Does this plan turn the frictions into consolidated habits for the users of the system?

title: Habitual E-mail Checking

part_a.trigger: The system uses an identical and indiscriminate visual design (same color, shape and behavior) for all interactive links, both for routine actions and for high-risk requests (Visual Flaw) AND allows the instantaneous execution of the action (single-click) just while the user is performing high-frequency repetitive tasks, such as rapid message routing (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (From the literature): An email client that displays the fraudulent link of a phishing email (e.g. "Solve the problem of your account by clicking here") with the classic blue or purple color underlined, identical in all respects to the secure links used daily, allowing immediate opening with a single click.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Social Media): A messaging app (e.g., WhatsApp or Facebook Messenger) in which links sent by compromised contacts instantly open the in-app browser with a single "tap," taking advantage of the user's compulsive habit of quickly scrolling and clicking content.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers Compulsive Behavior in its variant of automated habitual automaticity. Because checking emails or messages is such a frequently repeated action, it is stored as a "mental script." The user acts in a state of automaticity (lack of conscious attention and intentionality), feeling the irrepressible urge to "clean" the inbox or react to notifications.
part_a.error: The user physically clicks on the malicious link reflexively and instantaneously (e.g. in less than 1 second) as part of a habitual muscle sequence, instead of stopping to analytically inspect (Systematic Processing) the sender's address or the destination of the URL.
part_a.mitigation:
**Description**: Implement a "Behavioral Bundle" designed specifically to interrupt muscle memory (habitual pattern interruption).

**Ingredients**: Ingredient 1: Effort Asymmetry (Active Friction). When the user clicks on a link from an external or unverified sender, the system does not open the page immediately, but intercepts the click by inserting an intermediate screen (interstitial) that forces a wait of 3 seconds before the "Proceed" button becomes clickable., Ingredient 2: Social/Rule Cues. While waiting, the middle screen shows a policy text: "You are about to leave the protected environment. Automated systems cannot verify this external link. Please check the URL before proceeding."

part_b.audit_rule: Verifies whether the system uses an identical and indiscriminate visual design for routine and high-risk links/buttons (Visual Flaw) AND allows them to be executed instantaneously (single-click) during highly repetitive operations (e.g. mail/notification sorting), without introducing friction that breaks the routine (Timing/Context Flaw). [ ] Pass / [ ] Fail
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (Email/Web): Malicious links embedded in external emails that have the exact same visual formatting (underlined blue text) as secure internal links, and can be executed with a single click without any intermediate warning.
- Domain B (Mobile/Social): Messaging apps that open external links via in-app browsers with a single immediate "tap", indulging in compulsive scrolling of the feed.
- Domain C (Enterprise): Ticketing dashboard where the agent can open attachments provided by external customers with an instant double-click, just as they do for files uploaded by colleagues.
part_b.security_risk: This interface supports compulsive and automated behaviors (Habits/Automaticity). Users will process the task without executive control, physically clicking on dangerous links in a reflexive way even before Systematic Processing can detect the deception.
part_b.remediation: Interrupt the habit pattern interruption via a Behavioral Bundle. Enter an Active Friction: when you click on an external link, intercept the command with a pop-up that forces you to wait 3 seconds before enabling the confirm button. Add a Rule Cue: Visually explain to the user that friction is for inspecting an unverified external target.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the company require employees (e.g., customer service, secretaries) to handle huge volumes of emails with tight response times? This pushes the employee to rely on impulsive muscle automatisms to survive the workload, thwarting safety.

title: Compulsive Click Behavior Prevention by Active Friction

part_a.trigger: The system presents alarms or notifications with high anxiety/emergencies containing interactive visual elements for immediate resolution (Visual Flaw) AND allows them to be executed instantly and without friction (e.g. a clickable link or a direct button) right at the moment of maximum stress or uncertainty for the user (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (From the literature): A pandemic-themed phishing email that warns of "COVID-19 cases on the rise in your area" by presenting a large blue clickable "SEE NEW CASES IN YOUR AREA" button.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Banking Mobile App): A push notification on the phone that reads "Suspicious activity detected on the card" followed by a single direct "Verify Now" button that opens an external web page, without requiring prior login in the secure app.
- Example 3 (Generalization - Enterprise): A fake corporate IT alert that communicates "Account deactivation imminent" and includes a direct link to confirm credentials, taking advantage of the urgency of not losing access to work.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design activates Compulsive Behavior (specifically, compulsive checking and reassurance seeking). When faced with an ambiguous threat, the user experiences psychological distress and an uncontrollable urge to regain control of the situation. The presence of an immediate link offers a false and fast way to obtain the reassurance sought.
part_a.error: The user performs the physical action of clicking on the link or opening the attachment instantly (in less than 1 second) in an attempt to find reassurances or details, instead of performing the safe action of manually opening the official portal by typing the URL.
part_a.mitigation:
**Description**: Implement a "Behavioral Bundle" based on the neutralization of the automatic action.

**Ingredients**: Ingredient 1: Effort Asymmetry (Friction). The email client or OS system disables direct hyperlinks within messages classified as "high urgency" or from uncertified external senders. The user must physically copy and paste the URL or manually type in the destination., Ingredient 2: Social/Rule Cues. Instead of the clickable link, the system displays an explicit microcopy: "Security Policy: Deep links are disabled for security alerts. Please manually log in to your personal area to check this notification".

part_b.audit_rule: Verifies whether the system presents warnings or alert messages with a high emotional or emergency component (Visual Flaw) allowing the user an instant and direct interaction (e.g. a link or clickable button "Solve Now") without any friction or intermediate verification step at the moment of maximum stress (Timing/Context Flaw). [ ] Pass / [ ] Fail
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (Email/Web): An email that communicates a health/administrative emergency (e.g. "Increase in cases in your area") and provides a direct link to take action or inform yourself instantly.
- Domain B (Mobile): A system security alert that asks the user to verify suspicious activity on the account by offering only a generic and immediate button ("Check activity"), without going through biometric authentication.
- Domain C (Enterprise): Urgent messages from the fake corporate "Human Resources Department" requesting to download attachments (e.g. "Emergency Guidelines") by clicking on a featured zip file, bypassing the intranet.
part_b.security_risk: This design triggers compulsive behavior (reassurance seeking). Faced with the discomfort of a possible threat, the user will develop the impulse to obtain quick information and reassurance. He will end up performing the physical action of blindly clicking on the link, bypassing cognitive assessments altogether.
part_b.remediation: Implement a "Behavioral Bundle" of Friction + Rules. Disable direct clickability (hyperlink) for messages classified as urgent from external sources (Friction). Replace the link with static informational text accompanied by the business rule: "For security reasons, we do not provide direct links. Log in to your personal area by opening a new tab and typing the address" (Rule Cue).
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the company regularly use internal communications with urgent direct links (e.g., HR or IT communications)? This normalizes the habit of "quick clicking", nullifying the effectiveness of the defenses against phishing.

title: Preventing bypass of security controls

part_a.trigger: The system makes critical security controls optional (Visual Flaw) and allows users to skip them without any friction or verification, favoring rapid task completion over security (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): During the configuration of an enterprise Wi-Fi network, the system presents certificate verification as optional. Users can skip the check and connect quickly without any barrier, choosing the fastest but insecure option.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A mobile app requests access to sensitive permissions (e.g., location or microphone) and presents an immediate 'Allow' button, while advanced settings are hidden. The user grants access without reviewing the security implications.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design generates frustration because it exposes the user to unclear technical options without explicit guidance, making the secure path more complex and effortful. The increase in cognitive effort and decision uncertainty leads the user to reduce effort by choosing the fastest solution.
part_a.error: The user physically skips or bypasses security controls (e.g., certificate verification or permission review), selecting the fastest option instead of securely configuring the settings.
part_a.mitigation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle combining Effort Asymmetry, Response-Contingent Feedback, and Social/Rule Cues. The system should introduce friction for risky actions (e.g., mandatory confirmation or a short delay before proceeding), provide real-time explanations of available options to reduce uncertainty, and display microcopy explaining the rule (e.g., 'Security checks protect your device. Avoid skipping them.').

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system makes critical security controls optional and allows users to skip them without any friction or verification. Ensure that the secure path is not more complex or less accessible than the insecure one. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A (Networks): During enterprise Wi-Fi configuration, the user can skip certificate verification and connect immediately. | Domain B (Mobile): An app requests access to sensitive permissions by showing an immediate 'Allow' button, while security options are hidden. | Domain C (Software Installation): A system allows software installation without verifying certificates or digital signatures, offering a quick option to continue.
part_b.security_risk: The interface encourages impulsive and speed-oriented behaviors. Users bypass security controls to reduce effort, exposing the system to vulnerabilities, man-in-the-middle attacks, and unauthorized access.
part_b.remediation: Implement secure-by-default flows by introducing friction in risky actions (e.g., mandatory confirmation or delays) and providing real-time feedback and guidance. Use explanatory microcopy to clarify the importance of security controls.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization implicitly encourage execution speed over secure configuration, or does it provide adequate training on security controls?

title: Managing frustration in authentication policies

part_a.trigger: The system imposes complex and restrictive password requirements (Visual Flaw) and requires mandatory password changes during primary tasks, interrupting the user's workflow (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): A company system requires users to change their passwords every 30 days while they're performing work tasks. New passwords must meet complex constraints (capitalization, symbols, no reuse), blocking access until they're complete, causing disruption and frustration.
